title.en: Kein and nicht: two ways to say 'not'

summary.en: Use kein to negate an indefinite or bare noun, and nicht for verbs, adjectives, and specific nouns.

body.en:
From season 1, episode 1.

When Helga opens the mixed-up suitcase, she protests that it is *nicht* *mein Koffer* and that she certainly wears *keine Schuhe* in size forty-four, just after Martin complains that he cannot find *meine Brille* *nicht*. German splits English 'not / no' cleanly between *kein* and *nicht*.

Use *kein* wherever the positive sentence would have *ein* or no article at all: *ein Koffer* becomes *kein Koffer*, feminine singular takes *keine* (*keine Nachttischlampe*), and any plural bare noun also takes *keine* (*keine Schuhe*).

Use *nicht* to negate a verb, an adjective, or a noun that already has *der*, *die*, *das* or a possessive like *mein* (*nicht* *mein Koffer*, or clause-final *nicht* after *meine Brille*).

On replay, notice how *nicht* waits at the very end when Martin negates finding his glasses, while *keine* sits right in front of the noun.
